title: LENS: In-Context Search via Latent Evidence Exploration over Dynamic Raw Documents

visual_explainer.question: What changes when evidence is localized over raw dynamic documents at query time instead of being pre-materialized into fixed chunks and an index?
visual_explainer.takeaway: LENS keeps the evidence space latent until the query arrives, then iteratively proposes raw-document regions, observes LLM relevance, updates beliefs, and stops under a budget.
visual_explainer.compared_with: Pre-materialized indexed RAG and an index-free ReAct-style search baseline over the same raw corpus snapshot.

analysis.tldr: LENS moves evidence materialization from indexing time to query time: it treats raw-document regions as a latent evidence space and sequentially proposes, scores, and refines regions under a budget. Its strongest result is better evidence localization/grounding and immediate freshness after corpus changes—not better answer EM than a ReAct baseline, which is tied or slightly better in the main controlled settings.
analysis.problem: Fixed chunking and persistent indexes commit to evidence boundaries before the question is known and can become stale when raw documents change. The alternative—searching raw files at query time—needs a principled way to allocate a finite exploration budget rather than scanning blindly.
analysis.core_idea: Formulate Budgeted Evidence Localization over query-dependent raw-document windows. A low-cost prior proposes candidates from lexical, local, structural, or reusable evidence cues; an LLM relevance oracle observes raw text, updates per-fact beliefs, adapts proposal weights, and stops when requirements are resolved or the budget is exhausted. Retrieved regions are consolidated into source-grounded evidence.
analysis.agent_loop: build query-conditioned prior → propose lexical/local/exploratory raw-document regions → inspect with relevance oracle → update evidence beliefs and proposal weights → continue or stop under budget → consolidate grounded regions → answer
analysis.retrieval_design: LENS is index-free at query time over the raw document collection. It does not pre-materialize fixed evidence chunks; candidate boundaries and search focus are induced after the query. The sequential controller trades online LLM/search work for freshness and finer evidence localization.
compared_to: pre-indexed BM25/hybrid RAG under fresh and stale-index conditions
index-free ReAct-style search over matched corpus snapshots
ablations without the multi-signal prior or without sequential exploration
analysis.evidence: On the controlled 500-question evaluation, LENS reports 62.4% EM and 84.8% evidence recall versus 65.2% EM and 50.4% evidence recall for the ReAct-style baseline. On a fixed 150-question fullwiki raw-dump subset with zero indexing, answer EM is nearly tied (43.3% LENS vs 42.7% ReAct) while grounded answers are higher for LENS (84.0% vs 70.7%). Stale-index experiments show indexed baselines lose sharply after corpus changes, while index-free methods remain query-ready. The sequential-exploration ablation is the main contributor; removing the multi-signal prior does not reduce EM in the reported fullwiki ablation.
analysis.why_it_matters: LENS adds a second placement decision to the radar: not only where adaptivity lives, but when evidence itself is materialized. It extends raw-corpus interaction beyond fixed grep/read operations into query-conditioned region localization, while showing the real trade is freshness/grounding versus online compute rather than a clean answer-quality win.
limitations: The strongest answer-quality comparisons do not show a clear LENS win: ReAct is higher on D500 EM and essentially tied on fullwiki.
The method spends more online tokens and latency than ReAct in the reported controlled accounting, so zero indexing is not zero cost.
A closed-book reference remains strong on fullwiki, making parametric knowledge a material confound in final-answer attribution.
The evidence-localization gains are demonstrated on the paper's tested raw-document workloads; transfer to other document formats and interaction substrates remains open.
